results.question: What is the standard deduction?
results.reference_answer: The standard deduction is a fixed dollar amount that reduces taxable income, available instead of itemizing deductions like medical expenses and charitable contributions.
results.generated_answer:
# What is the Standard Deduction?

The standard deduction is a dollar amount that reduces your taxable income. [IRS Publication 17 (2025)](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p17.pdf) It eliminates the need for many taxpayers to itemize actual deductions, such as medical expenses, charitable contributions, and taxes, on Schedule A (Form 1040). [IRS Publication 17 (2025)](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p17.pdf)

## 2025 Standard Deduction Amounts

The standard deduction depends on your filing status:

- **Single**: $15,750 [IRS Revenue Procedure 2024-40 (2025 inflation adjustments)](https://www.irs.gov/credits-and-deductions-for-individuals)
- **Married Filing Jointly**: $31,500 [IRS Revenue Procedure 2024-40 (2025 inflation adjustments)](https://www.irs.gov/credits-and-deductions-for-individuals)
- **Married Filing Separately**: $15,750 [IRS Revenue Procedure 2024-40 (2025 inflation adjustments)](https://www.irs.gov/credits-and-deductions-for-individuals)
- **Head of Household**: $23,625 [IRS Revenue Procedure 2024-40 (2025 inflation adjustments)](https://www.irs.gov/credits-and-deductions-for-individuals)

## Additional Amounts

If you are **65 or older or blind**, you can claim an additional standard deduction: [IRS Publication 17 (2025)](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p17.pdf)

- **Single or Head of Household**: $2,000 [IRS Revenue Procedure 2024-40 (2025 inflation adjustments)](https://www.irs.gov/credits-and-deductions-for-individuals)
- **Married (per qualifying spouse)**: $1,600 [IRS Revenue Procedure 2024-40 (2025 inflation adjustments)](https://www.irs.gov/credits-and-deductions-for-individuals)

## Enhanced Deduction for Seniors (New for 2025)

Taxpayers who are age 65 or older may be eligible for an enhanced deduction for seniors of up to **$6,000 per person**. [IRS Publication 17 (2025)](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p17.pdf) This amount phases out above certain income thresholds. [IRS Revenue Procedure 2024-40 (2025 inflation adjustments)](https://www.irs.gov/credits-and-deductions-for-individuals)

## How It Works

You can choose to take the standard deduction or itemize your deductions, whichever method gives you the lower tax. [IRS Publication 17 (2025)](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p17.pdf)

This is general information, not personalized tax advice.

results.question: How does the law define gross income?
results.reference_answer: Gross income means all income from whatever source derived, as defined in 26 U.S.C. Section 61, unless specifically excluded elsewhere in the code.
results.generated_answer:
# Definition of Gross Income

According to federal tax law, **gross income means all income from whatever source derived** [section_61(a)]. This includes:

- Compensation for services (fees, commissions, fringe benefits) [section_61(a)(1)]
- Business income [section_61(a)(2)]
- Gains from property dealings [section_61(a)(3)]
- Interest, rents, royalties, dividends [section_61(a)(4)-(7)]
- Annuities, pensions, and partnership income [section_61(a)(8), (10), (12)]
- Income from discharge of indebtedness [section_61(a)(11)]
- Other sources listed in the tax code [section_61(a)(13)-(14)]

More broadly, **gross income is all income in the form of money, property, and services that isn't exempt from tax**, including income from sources outside the United States or from the sale of your main home (even if you can exclude part or all of it) [IRS Publication 17 (2025)](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p17.pdf).

Some specific items are excluded from gross income—see Internal Revenue Code Part III (sections 101 and following) for those exclusions [section_61(b)].

This is general information, not personalized tax advice.
results.judge_reasoning: Generated answer correctly states the core definition ("all income from whatever source derived") and references Section 61, matching the reference answer's key facts.

results.question: How is taxable income defined under the tax code?
results.reference_answer: Taxable income means gross income minus the deductions allowed by the chapter, including (for those who itemize) or excluding (for those who take the standard deduction) certain deductions, per Section 63.

# How Taxable Income is Defined

Under the tax code, **taxable income** is defined as:

**Gross income minus allowable deductions** [26 U.S. Code § 63](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/63)

More specifically, for individuals who don't itemize deductions (the most common case), taxable income equals:

- **Adjusted gross income**, minus:
  - The standard deduction [26 U.S. Code § 63](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/63)
  - The deduction for personal exemptions [26 U.S. Code § 63](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/63)

The standard deduction varies by filing status. For tax year 2025, the basic standard deductions are: [IRS Revenue Procedure 2024-40 (2025 inflation adjustments)](https://www.irs.gov/credits-and-deductions-for-individuals)
- Single: $15,750
- Married filing jointly: $31,500
- Head of household: $23,625

Additionally, those age 65 or older or blind may claim an additional standard deduction [IRS Revenue Procedure 2024-40 (2025 inflation adjustments)](https://www.irs.gov/credits-and-deductions-for-individuals), and there is a new enhanced senior deduction of $6,000 per person for 2025 (with income phase-out limits) [IRS Revenue Procedure 2024-40 (2025 inflation adjustments)](https://www.irs.gov/credits-and-deductions-for-individuals).

**This is general information, not personalized tax advice.**

results.question: What is a Self-Select PIN used for when e-filing?

**What it is:** A Self-Select PIN is any combination of five digits you choose (except five zeros) that you create yourself to sign your return electronically [IRS Publication 17 (2025)](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p17.pdf).

**When you use it:** You must use the Self-Select PIN method if you're filing online using tax software. If you're using a tax practitioner, you can choose between a Self-Select PIN or a Practitioner PIN [IRS Publication 17 (2025)](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p17.pdf).

- Your PIN

results.question: Who can I claim as a dependent on my tax return?
results.reference_answer: Dependents are defined under 26 U.S.C. Section 152, which sets out qualifying child and qualifying relative rules, among other requirements.
results.generated_answer:
# Who Can You Claim as a Dependent

You can claim someone as a dependent if they meet the requirements and fall into one of these categories [IRS Publication 17 (2025)](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p17.pdf):

- **A qualifying child**, or
- **A qualifying relative**

## Three Key Tests

Even if someone is a qualifying child or relative, you can only claim them as a dependent if all three of these tests are met [IRS Publication 17 (2025)](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p17.pdf):

1. **Dependent Taxpayer Test** — You can't claim anyone as a dependent if you yourself can be claimed as a dependent by another taxpayer (with limited exceptions)
2. **Joint Return Test** — You generally can't claim a married person who files a joint return as a dependent, unless that joint return is filed only to claim a refund of withheld or estimated tax
3. **Citizen or Resident Test** — The person must be a U.S. citizen, U.S. resident alien, U.S. national, or a resident of Canada or Mexico [IRS Publication 17 (2025)](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p17.pdf)

## Who You Can't Claim

You can't claim housekeepers, maids, or servants as dependents, even if they meet other requirements [IRS Publication 17 (2025)](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p17.pdf).

The context provided doesn't include the detailed definitions of "qualifying child" and "qualifying relative," so for complete information on who qualifies under those categories, consult IRS Publication 501.

results.question: Should I take the standard deduction or itemize?

# Should You Take the Standard Deduction or Itemize?

You should **itemize deductions if your total itemized deductions are more than your standard deduction amount.** [IRS Publication 17 (2025)](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p17.pdf) Compare the two amounts and use whichever gives you the greater tax benefit.

## When Itemizing May Benefit You

You may benefit from itemizing if you: [IRS Publication 17 (2025)](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p17.pdf)
- Had large uninsured medical and dental expenses during the year
- Paid interest and taxes on your home
- Had large uninsured casualty or theft losses
- Made significant charitable contributions

## Your Standard Deduction Amount (2025)

For reference, the 2025 standard deduction amounts are: [IRS Revenue Procedure 2024-40 (2025 inflation adjustments)](https://www.irs.gov/credits-and-deductions-for-individuals)
- **Single**: $15,750
- **Married Filing Jointly**: $31,500
- **Married Filing Separately**: $15,750
- **Head of Household**: $23,625

If you're 65 or older or blind, you may qualify for an additional standard deduction of $2,000 (single/head of household) or $1,600 per qualifying spouse (married). [IRS Revenue Procedure 2024-40 (2025 inflation adjustments)](https://www.irs.gov/credits-and-deductions-for-individuals)

## Important Note

Even if your itemized deductions are less than your standard deduction, you can still elect to itemize if it benefits your state tax return. [IRS Publication 17 (2025)](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p17.pdf)

**This is general information, not personalized tax advice.**
